medical.title: Dad's antidepressant use linked to higher metabolic disorder risk in children
medical.summary: Use of antidepressants by fathers in the months just before pregnancy is associated with a slightly increased risk of metabolic disorders, particularly high blood pressure, in their children, finds a large study from Denmark published by The BMJ.

medical.title: ADHD meds in pregnancy not linked to developmental disorders in children
medical.summary: Children born to mothers who used attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) medication during pregnancy face no increased risk of neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism, ADHD, intellectual disability and learning disorders, finds a large Scandinavian study published by The BMJ.

medical.title: Genetic information can improve prostate cancer risk assessment
medical.summary: Genetic information can help provide a more individual assessment of prostate cancer risk among men undergoing PSA testing, according to a new study from Karolinska Institutet published in JAMA Network Open. PSA is a protein produced by the prostate that can be measured with a blood test. An elevated PSA level can be a sign of prostate cancer, but PSA levels can also be affected by other changes in the prostate.

medical.title: Membrane developed for dry eye treatment can improve symptoms
medical.summary: A study led by Aston University's Travé Huarte has shown that a new single six-day treatment for moderate to severe dry eye disease using a modified, windowed amniotic membrane can deliver sustained symptom relief with good treatment compliance.

medical.title: Novel hormone therapy significantly reduces risk of breast cancer recurrence
medical.summary: A new type of hormone therapy significantly reduced the risk of invasive breast cancer recurrence or death in patients with early-stage, hormone receptor (HR)-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer compared with standard treatments, according to findings from a large international phase 3 clinical trial co-led by investigators at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

medical.title: Youth are turning to AI for mental health support. Here's what families should know
medical.summary: There are few areas in life where AI isn't shaking things up. And managing mental health is no exception.

medical.title: RSV shots safe for older adults, alone or in combo, analysis finds
medical.summary: Multiple clinical trials have found that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines are safe in adults. Now, a new study in people age 60 and older shows it's also safe to receive an RSV shot plus another vaccine in the same week.

medical.title: Study suggests BMI alone may miss obesity-related dementia risk
medical.summary: A newer way of defining obesity that looks beyond body mass index (BMI) may identify more older adults with an increased risk of dementia than BMI alone, according to a study published Nov. 25, 2026, in Neurology.

medical.title: Same oncogenic mutation, different outcomes: Why some blood vessels develop malformations while others remain resistant
medical.summary: Why do certain cancer-associated mutations cause malformations in some blood vessels while leaving others largely unaffected? The answer lies in the identity and developmental stage of endothelial cells, the cells lining the inside of blood vessels.

medical.title: Date-rape drug GHB disappears within hours, but molecular trace could reveal use two days later
medical.summary: GHB has long posed a major challenge for the criminal justice system. The substance is eliminated from the body so quickly that proving cases of drugging and drug-facilitated rape can be extremely difficult. Now, researchers at Aarhus University have made a crucial discovery.

medical.title: Early-life stress may leave lasting traces in the brain that increase risk of chronic pain
medical.summary: Researchers from the Heidelberg Faculty of Medicine of Heidelberg University and the Central Institute of Mental Health (ZI) in Mannheim have identified a neural mechanism in female mice through which early-life stress may increase vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety disorders. The findings have been published in the journal Science.

medical.title: AI could identify psoriasis and assess its severity from a single photo
medical.summary: Widely available artificial intelligence models could not only recognize psoriasis from a single photo but also assess its severity, according to an international study by researchers at Semmelweis University. The study, published in Frontiers in Medicine, found that ChatGPT-5 identified the skin condition and correctly assessed its severity with nearly 100% accuracy. However, the researchers caution that, despite the promising results, artificial intelligence cannot replace dermatologists, and anyone experiencing symptoms should seek professional medical advice.

medical.title: Alzheimer's drug targets tau protein in promising clinical trial
medical.summary: An experimental Alzheimer's drug that reduces the production of a protein called tau has slowed the decline in memory and thinking skills by up to 54% in a clinical trial.

medical.title: Smoking injures the placenta early in pregnancy, study shows
medical.summary: It is well known that women who smoke during pregnancy put their unborn babies at risk of being born prematurely or with low birth weight. Tobacco smoke can also injure a growing baby's organs.

medical.title: How appreciating nature can make life feel more meaningful
medical.summary: Spending time outdoors can influence how a person feels, but researchers at Texas A&M University wanted to understand why.

medical.title: Teenage girls more in tune with their bodies tend to be happier with how they look
medical.summary: Teenage girls who are better at recognizing signals from inside their bodies tend to be happier with how they look, according to new research.

medical.title: Patients in Indian clinic were well served by standard WHO-recommended HIV treatment, study finds
medical.summary: A McGill-led study of HIV patients in Pune, India, who received the tenofovir, lamivudine and dolutegravir (TLD) drug regimen found no improvement in outcomes for those who received versions of the treatment tailored to their personal characteristics.

medical.title: Brain organoids in space reveal new clues to Alzheimer's disease
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have found that spaceflight alters biological processes associated with Alzheimer's disease in different ways depending on genetic background. The study, published on Nov. 25, 2026, in Science Advances, suggests space could reveal changes in brain cells that are difficult to detect on Earth.

medical.title: Mindfulness is linked to better mental health and more beneficial social media use
medical.summary: Mindfulness is associated with better mental health and with more beneficial patterns of social media use, according to a review published Nov. 25, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Marc Tibber and Charlotte Jones from University College London, United Kingdom.

medical.title: Potential limits of breast cancer screening policies across Southeast Asia identified
medical.summary: In Southeast Asia, breast cancer screening could have limited potential to reduce breast cancer mortality due to screening age eligibility not aligning with the actual ages at which women develop the disease, according to a study by the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine).

medical.title: Protein quality control helps regulate circadian rhythms, study suggests
medical.summary: The body's internal circadian clock helps us feel sleepy at night and wake up in the morning. Using fruit flies, researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have discovered that a cellular quality control process that removes defective proteins during protein synthesis helps regulate the pace of the circadian clock.

medical.title: PET/CT imaging provides new insights into type 1 diabetes progression
medical.summary: A novel molecular imaging approach that measures beta-cell mass in the pancreas can offer valuable insights into the progression of type 1 diabetes, according to new research published in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine. The study found that individuals who have had type 1 diabetes for less than seven years have higher total beta-cell mass and function, larger pancreatic volume and lower intrapancreatic fat compared to those who have had the disease for longer. This valuable information, paired with functional tests, has the potential to significantly improve clinical trials of new therapeutic interventions.

medical.title: Lab-grown brain model may accelerate development of safer, longer-lasting brain implants
medical.summary: Researchers have developed a laboratory cell model that mimics how the brain reacts to implanted devices, potentially offering a faster, lower-cost and more ethical way to test neural implants.

medical.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
medical.summary: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.

medical.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
medical.summary: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

science.title: Minecraft-like DNA cubes self-assemble into complex 3D nanostructures
science.summary: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system that could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics and next-generation nanotechnology.

science.title: Stabilizing atomically thin metals with sandwich structures: Machine learning expands the search
science.summary: Atomically thin metals, metallenes, are promising materials for catalysis, electronics and energy conversion, but their synthesis has been challenging. Researchers from the University of Jyväskylä have now identified more than 300 stable metallene sandwich structures using machine learning and high-performance computing. The results provide researchers with a practical roadmap for the fabrication of new two-dimensional metals.

science.title: Smartphone app uses AI to identify illegal wildlife products
science.summary: Illegal and unsustainable wildlife trade is a major driver of biodiversity loss. Thousands of animal species are traded, along with products made from them, ranging from ivory to scales and powders.

science.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
science.summary: Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. The researchers discovered how certain fungi promote the formation of new water-conducting cells in plants. At the same time, infected plants showed increased tolerance to drought stress. The results were published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe.

science.title: Carbon nanotube measurements reveal quantum model better explains collective electron behavior
science.summary: An international team of scientists from Lithuania, Finland and Israel has conducted both theoretical and experimental research into carbon nanotubes, becoming the first to demonstrate which physical model governs the motion and interactions of electrons within them.

science.title: Five reasons why we should still make things with our hands
science.summary: It's 7 a.m. Still dark outside. "Alex, time to wake up! You have a busy day ahead, with an important meeting at 8:30," announces the alarm in a soft but firm voice. Alex wakes up immediately, already thinking about the presentation that still needs a few finishing touches. In the kitchen, the coffee machine, set up for 7 a.m. sharp, has just finished brewing. "Alexa, set the temperature to 20 degrees," says Alex, reaching for the coffee.

science.title: New inhibitor restores antibiotic activity against drug-resistant bacteria
science.summary: Researchers from Imperial College London and collaborators have identified a potent small-molecule inhibitor that can restore the activity of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

science.title: NASA's Europa Clipper zooming by Earth on way to Jupiter's icy moon
science.summary: NASA's Europa Clipper will soon swing past Earth before making a yearslong beeline for Jupiter, where the orbiter will probe whether the ocean beneath its moon Europa's icy shell has the ingredients for life. The flyby will offer a propellant-saving boost and an opportunity to prepare for the science-gathering that lies ahead.

science.title: Shopping as a 'collector' makes us want to buy more, new research shows
science.summary: Shoppers are more likely to buy products and pay more for them when they adopt a "collecting mindset," according to new research co-authored by Bayes Business School (City St George's, University of London).

science.title: Giant lambda-shaped stellar nursery found in the Milky Way's outskirts
science.summary: Massive stars often form in dense regions, called "hubs," where filamentary structures made of star-forming materials meet. These star-forming complexes are "hub-filament" systems. Astronomers have discovered one such large network of molecular gas filaments in the outer regions of the Milky Way. It is called the λ-complex, and the structure is bigger than most known hub-filament systems. The research paper was published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on Nov. 17.

science.title: Sustainable procurement in multinational corporations depends on people and the operating environment
science.summary: Elizabeth Jeromaa's doctoral dissertation in management, to be examined at the University of Vaasa, demonstrates that it is possible for companies to implement environmentally sustainable procurement practices, though there is no one-size-fits-all model.

science.title: Heaven scent: Study shows link between a partner's body odor and sexual intimacy
science.summary: Many people spend a considerable amount of time and money trying to disguise their natural body odor. But not everyone finds our natural scent unpleasant. In fact, it could be part of what makes a couple click.

science.title: Using lunar craters as free radiation shields for moon base nuclear reactors
science.summary: Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the moon.

science.title: Without marine life, atmospheric CO₂ would shoot up by up to 65% by the end of the century
science.summary: Without marine organisms transporting carbon into the deep ocean, the accumulation of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere would be drastically higher in the year 2100, reaching levels between 35% and 65% higher than projected. This is one of the main conclusions of the new policy brief developed within the framework of the European OceanICU project, which was presented at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

science.title: Structural agility of 2D crystals enables digital doping of graphene superlattices

mix_items.title: RSV shots safe for older adults, alone or in combo, analysis finds
mix_items.summary: Multiple clinical trials have found that respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines are safe in adults. Now, a new study in people age 60 and older shows it's also safe to receive an RSV shot plus another vaccine in the same week.

mix_items.title: Smartphone app uses AI to identify illegal wildlife products
mix_items.summary: Illegal and unsustainable wildlife trade is a major driver of biodiversity loss. Thousands of animal species are traded, along with products made from them, ranging from ivory to scales and powders.

mix_items.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
mix_items.summary: Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. The researchers discovered how certain fungi promote the formation of new water-conducting cells in plants. At the same time, infected plants showed increased tolerance to drought stress. The results were published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe.

mix_items.title: Carbon nanotube measurements reveal quantum model better explains collective electron behavior
mix_items.summary: An international team of scientists from Lithuania, Finland and Israel has conducted both theoretical and experimental research into carbon nanotubes, becoming the first to demonstrate which physical model governs the motion and interactions of electrons within them.

mix_items.title: Study suggests BMI alone may miss obesity-related dementia risk
mix_items.summary: A newer way of defining obesity that looks beyond body mass index (BMI) may identify more older adults with an increased risk of dementia than BMI alone, according to a study published Nov. 25, 2026, in Neurology.

mix_items.title: Same oncogenic mutation, different outcomes: Why some blood vessels develop malformations while others remain resistant
mix_items.summary: Why do certain cancer-associated mutations cause malformations in some blood vessels while leaving others largely unaffected? The answer lies in the identity and developmental stage of endothelial cells, the cells lining the inside of blood vessels.

mix_items.title: Five reasons why we should still make things with our hands
mix_items.summary: It's 7 a.m. Still dark outside. "Alex, time to wake up! You have a busy day ahead, with an important meeting at 8:30," announces the alarm in a soft but firm voice. Alex wakes up immediately, already thinking about the presentation that still needs a few finishing touches. In the kitchen, the coffee machine, set up for 7 a.m. sharp, has just finished brewing. "Alexa, set the temperature to 20 degrees," says Alex, reaching for the coffee.

mix_items.title: New inhibitor restores antibiotic activity against drug-resistant bacteria
mix_items.summary: Researchers from Imperial College London and collaborators have identified a potent small-molecule inhibitor that can restore the activity of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

mix_items.title: Date-rape drug GHB disappears within hours, but molecular trace could reveal use two days later
mix_items.summary: GHB has long posed a major challenge for the criminal justice system. The substance is eliminated from the body so quickly that proving cases of drugging and drug-facilitated rape can be extremely difficult. Now, researchers at Aarhus University have made a crucial discovery.

mix_items.title: NASA's Europa Clipper zooming by Earth on way to Jupiter's icy moon
mix_items.summary: NASA's Europa Clipper will soon swing past Earth before making a yearslong beeline for Jupiter, where the orbiter will probe whether the ocean beneath its moon Europa's icy shell has the ingredients for life. The flyby will offer a propellant-saving boost and an opportunity to prepare for the science-gathering that lies ahead.

mix_items.title: Shopping as a 'collector' makes us want to buy more, new research shows
mix_items.summary: Shoppers are more likely to buy products and pay more for them when they adopt a "collecting mindset," according to new research co-authored by Bayes Business School (City St George's, University of London).

mix_items.title: Early-life stress may leave lasting traces in the brain that increase risk of chronic pain
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Heidelberg Faculty of Medicine of Heidelberg University and the Central Institute of Mental Health (ZI) in Mannheim have identified a neural mechanism in female mice through which early-life stress may increase vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety disorders. The findings have been published in the journal Science.

mix_items.title: AI could identify psoriasis and assess its severity from a single photo
mix_items.summary: Widely available artificial intelligence models could not only recognize psoriasis from a single photo but also assess its severity, according to an international study by researchers at Semmelweis University. The study, published in Frontiers in Medicine, found that ChatGPT-5 identified the skin condition and correctly assessed its severity with nearly 100% accuracy. However, the researchers caution that, despite the promising results, artificial intelligence cannot replace dermatologists, and anyone experiencing symptoms should seek professional medical advice.

mix_items.title: Giant lambda-shaped stellar nursery found in the Milky Way's outskirts
mix_items.summary: Massive stars often form in dense regions, called "hubs," where filamentary structures made of star-forming materials meet. These star-forming complexes are "hub-filament" systems. Astronomers have discovered one such large network of molecular gas filaments in the outer regions of the Milky Way. It is called the λ-complex, and the structure is bigger than most known hub-filament systems. The research paper was published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on Nov. 17.

mix_items.title: Alzheimer's drug targets tau protein in promising clinical trial
mix_items.summary: An experimental Alzheimer's drug that reduces the production of a protein called tau has slowed the decline in memory and thinking skills by up to 54% in a clinical trial.

mix_items.title: Sustainable procurement in multinational corporations depends on people and the operating environment
mix_items.summary: Elizabeth Jeromaa's doctoral dissertation in management, to be examined at the University of Vaasa, demonstrates that it is possible for companies to implement environmentally sustainable procurement practices, though there is no one-size-fits-all model.

mix_items.title: Heaven scent: Study shows link between a partner's body odor and sexual intimacy
mix_items.summary: Many people spend a considerable amount of time and money trying to disguise their natural body odor. But not everyone finds our natural scent unpleasant. In fact, it could be part of what makes a couple click.

mix_items.title: Smoking injures the placenta early in pregnancy, study shows
mix_items.summary: It is well known that women who smoke during pregnancy put their unborn babies at risk of being born prematurely or with low birth weight. Tobacco smoke can also injure a growing baby's organs.

mix_items.title: Using lunar craters as free radiation shields for moon base nuclear reactors
mix_items.summary: Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the moon.

mix_items.title: How appreciating nature can make life feel more meaningful
mix_items.summary: Spending time outdoors can influence how a person feels, but researchers at Texas A&M University wanted to understand why.

mix_items.title: Teenage girls more in tune with their bodies tend to be happier with how they look
mix_items.summary: Teenage girls who are better at recognizing signals from inside their bodies tend to be happier with how they look, according to new research.

mix_items.title: Without marine life, atmospheric CO₂ would shoot up by up to 65% by the end of the century
mix_items.summary: Without marine organisms transporting carbon into the deep ocean, the accumulation of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere would be drastically higher in the year 2100, reaching levels between 35% and 65% higher than projected. This is one of the main conclusions of the new policy brief developed within the framework of the European OceanICU project, which was presented at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

mix_items.title: Structural agility of 2D crystals enables digital doping of graphene superlattices
mix_items.summary: A study published in Nature has demonstrated that applying an electric field can switch the atomic arrangement in a stack of two-dimensional (2D) crystals, accompanied by an unusual charge behavior. This provides a new experimental platform for exploring how the structural and electronic properties of atomically thin materials interact.

mix_items.title: Patients in Indian clinic were well served by standard WHO-recommended HIV treatment, study finds
mix_items.summary: A McGill-led study of HIV patients in Pune, India, who received the tenofovir, lamivudine and dolutegravir (TLD) drug regimen found no improvement in outcomes for those who received versions of the treatment tailored to their personal characteristics.

mix_items.title: NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement
mix_items.summary: How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE […]

mix_items.title: Uterine pressure guides head-to-tail axis formation in mouse embryos
mix_items.summary: During animal development, the establishment of the three primary body axes—head-to-tail (anterior-posterior), dorsal-ventral and left-right—is essential for building a proper body structure. A fertilized egg, initially a single cell, undergoes repeated cell divisions to form a multicellular structure called an embryo, and body axes are formed within the embryo.

mix_items.title: Weak oversight and financial incentives may fuel health care corruption, review finds
mix_items.summary: Corruption in health systems may arise when governance failures offer opportunities and systemic vulnerabilities provide incentives for private gain, according to an umbrella review published in the open-access journal PLOS Global Public Health by Michele Coleman and Petra Varkonyi from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, United Kingdom, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Brain organoids in space reveal new clues to Alzheimer's disease
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have found that spaceflight alters biological processes associated with Alzheimer's disease in different ways depending on genetic background. The study, published on Nov. 25, 2026, in Science Advances, suggests space could reveal changes in brain cells that are difficult to detect on Earth.

mix_items.title: The triple helix: How a rare twist in human evolution may influence fetal cooling
mix_items.summary: The human umbilical cord is an evolutionary rarity, with the arrangement of blood vessels within its distinctive twisted structure potentially helping unborn babies stay cool in the womb, according to a team led by University of Manchester and University of Southampton scientists.

mix_items.title: Mapping the uncharted plate tectonic cycle: The hidden path from plate destruction to new oceanic crust
mix_items.summary: Since the discovery of plate tectonics, the ultimate fate of the massive plates that sink into Earth's interior mantle at subduction zones has remained a major geological quest. Meanwhile, magma continuously rises from the deep mantle to form new oceanic crust, erupting as mid-ocean ridge basalts (MORB).

mix_items.title: Errors in judging friendships predict who will connect or drift apart six months later
mix_items.summary: Decades of research show that mental representations of social networks are riddled with errors, with people commonly misidentifying existing ties and reporting relationships that do not exist. While these inaccuracies have been interpreted as noise arising from the limits of memory or attention, Brown University researchers have discovered a much more intriguing explanation: These "errors" are accurate representations of social connections that just haven't happened yet.

mix_items.title: Evolution's balancing act—keeping genes in sync after genome duplication
mix_items.summary: Getting the right balance is important in all walks of life, whether it's a healthy combination of food groups in a balanced diet or a balanced mix of skills that allows a work or sports team to succeed.

mix_items.title: Mindfulness is linked to better mental health and more beneficial social media use
mix_items.summary: Mindfulness is associated with better mental health and with more beneficial patterns of social media use, according to a review published Nov. 25, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Marc Tibber and Charlotte Jones from University College London, United Kingdom.

mix_items.title: The birds are listening: Seabirds reveal hidden fishing activity at sea
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of Oxford fitted miniature audio recorders and GPS trackers to seabirds to better understand the impacts of fishing boats on wildlife. This revealed that seabirds may be interacting with human vessels considerably more than official tracking data suggest. The results have been published on Nov. 25 in Science Advances.

mix_items.title: Antidiscrimination laws in US often lack clear wording relevant to multiracial identities
mix_items.summary: A new analysis highlights the limited appearance of the phrases "perceived race" and "multiracial" in U.S. federal and state antidiscrimination laws and demonstrates how court cases can be analyzed to explore whether such wording contributes to ambiguity that may hamper equal protection of multiracial people. Victoria Jackson and colleagues at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, U.S., present these findings in the journal PLOS One on Nov. 25, 2026.

mix_items.title: Potential limits of breast cancer screening policies across Southeast Asia identified
mix_items.summary: In Southeast Asia, breast cancer screening could have limited potential to reduce breast cancer mortality due to screening age eligibility not aligning with the actual ages at which women develop the disease, according to a study by the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine).

mix_items.title: Protein quality control helps regulate circadian rhythms, study suggests
mix_items.summary: The body's internal circadian clock helps us feel sleepy at night and wake up in the morning. Using fruit flies, researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have discovered that a cellular quality control process that removes defective proteins during protein synthesis helps regulate the pace of the circadian clock.

mix_items.title: PET/CT imaging provides new insights into type 1 diabetes progression
mix_items.summary: A novel molecular imaging approach that measures beta-cell mass in the pancreas can offer valuable insights into the progression of type 1 diabetes, according to new research published in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine. The study found that individuals who have had type 1 diabetes for less than seven years have higher total beta-cell mass and function, larger pancreatic volume and lower intrapancreatic fat compared to those who have had the disease for longer. This valuable information, paired with functional tests, has the potential to significantly improve clinical trials of new therapeutic interventions.

mix_items.title: Lab-grown brain model may accelerate development of safer, longer-lasting brain implants
mix_items.summary: Researchers have developed a laboratory cell model that mimics how the brain reacts to implanted devices, potentially offering a faster, lower-cost and more ethical way to test neural implants.

mix_items.title: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus
mix_items.summary: As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. mix_items.summary: Suncor, Canada’s second-largest oil company, wants to release treated wastewater from mining oil in Alberta’s tar sands into a drinking water source for the community of Fort Chipewyan. mix_items.summary: Tadeu de Oliveira, founder and leader of the Tiger Cats Conservation Initiative, a group of scientists committed to studying the smallest wildcats of South and Central America, wanted to be crystal clear: “It is rare to catch a tiger cat. mix_items.title: Ecuador’s bioeconomy plan vows sustainability, but faces a test of government priorities
mix_items.summary: The government of Ecuador has approved a new 10-year plan to promote economic activities that make use of the country’s biological resources, while also taking steps to conserve the ecosystems that they rely on. It aims to innovate agribusiness, ecotourism, and other industries in rural areas, without threatening the environment or Indigenous communities. The National […]

mix_items.title: As new season starts, Antarctic krill-fishing vessels face urgent conservation decision (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Despite promising developments, the 27 member states of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) have again failed to reach an agreement that protects the Southern Ocean. Mired by consensus decision-making and shrouded from public view by confidentiality rules, Antarctica’s governance systems are no longer fulfilling their mandate. This leaves room […]

mix_items.title: In the Bolivian Andes, Indigenous women plant native trees to restore water sources
mix_items.summary: The bare ridges of the Tunari mountain range rise high in Bolivia’s central Cochabamba department. Only the occasional stand of squat, shrubby trees and rust-red potato crops dot the slopes. It wasn’t always this way. The high-elevation landscape was once filled with native Kewiña (Polylepis sp.) trees, a slow-growing tree belonging to the rose family […]

mix_items.summary: ANATALYA, Türkiye — A year ago, a record number of Indigenous people attended the United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil. Although there as observers, without a seat at the negotiating table, they left with promises: recognition of their lands, a share of a new forest fund, and a just transition mechanism in the making. mix_items.summary: EDINBURGH — Ocean conservation efforts are being hindered by inadequate funding, as well as difficulties translating research into action, according to attendees of an international marine conservation congress in Scotland. mix_items.title: Indonesia fires test palm oil certification scheme as NGOs question RSPO accountability
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — Environmental groups are questioning the effectiveness of a global organization that develops standards and certification for sustainable palm oil production after fires affected thousands of hectares in concessions belonging to its members in Indonesia — including areas certified under its sustainability scheme. The criticism came as the organization, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm […]

mix_items.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
mix_items.summary: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.

mix_items.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
mix_items.summary: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
